checks.question: Are there protected actions, data reads/writes, admin routes, background jobs, or APIs that can be reached without any authentication / identity verification, where public access was not an explicit, intended decision? (IAM-001)

onYes.title: Fix missing authentication (IAM-001): require identity before protected operations
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Endpoints/actions that expose or modify protected data without authentication let anonymous callers read or change data.

Find all instances: Enumerate routes/handlers/jobs/APIs and identify which require authentication. Look for endpoints lacking an [Authorize]/auth middleware/guard, internal admin routes, and background triggers reachable externally. Compare against which should be public.

Fix correctly: Require authentication before protected operations using the project's existing auth middleware/attributes. Make any genuinely public endpoint explicitly opt-in (e.g. an explicit AllowAnonymous marker) so the default is secure.

Constraints: Do not break legitimately public endpoints. Default to secure (deny by default).

Acceptance: Every protected operation requires authentication; public access is explicit. Add a test asserting an unauthenticated request to a protected endpoint is rejected (401).

checks.question: Does the codebase read/write/delete objects identified by a user-controlled ID without verifying the caller owns or is permitted to access that specific object (broken object-level authorization / IDOR)? (IAM-002)

onYes.title: Fix broken object-level authorization (IAM-002): check ownership per object
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Handlers that fetch/modify a resource by ID without an ownership/permission check let an authenticated user access other users' data by changing the ID (BOLA/IDOR).

Find all instances: Search for handlers that load a resource by a request-supplied ID, slug, or key and then act on it. Check whether each verifies the current principal's permission for that specific object (not just that they are logged in).

Fix correctly: On every object access, verify the caller is authorized for that exact object (e.g. scope the query by owner/tenant, or check a policy after load). Prefer scoping the data query so unauthorized objects are never returned.

Constraints: Apply consistently across read, write, and delete. Centralize the authorization check where possible (see IAM-020).

Acceptance: Every object access enforces per-object authorization. Add a test where user A requests user B's object ID and is denied (403/404).

checks.question: Do privileged actions rely only on UI hiding, route naming, client-side checks, or merely being authenticated, rather than enforcing a role/capability/policy check server-side (broken function-level authorization)? (IAM-003)

onYes.title: Fix broken function-level authorization (IAM-003): enforce role/policy server-side
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Privileged functions protected only by client-side hiding or generic authentication can be invoked directly by any authenticated user.

Find all instances: Search for admin/privileged endpoints and actions; verify each enforces a server-side role/capability/policy check, not just authentication or UI gating.

Fix correctly: Add server-side authorization (role/permission/policy) to every privileged function. Default deny; require explicit permission.

Constraints: Do not rely on the client. Centralize policy decisions (see IAM-020).

Acceptance: Privileged functions enforce server-side authorization. Add a test where a non-privileged authenticated user calling a privileged endpoint is denied (403).

checks.question: Does the codebase trust client-supplied authority-bearing fields (role, tenant, owner, isAdmin, permission, price, status, or similar) when binding requests or persisting entities, allowing privilege escalation via mutable fields? (IAM-004)

onYes.title: Fix mass-assignment privilege escalation (IAM-004): ignore client authority fields
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Binding requests directly into entities lets a user set role/owner/tenant/price/status fields and escalate privileges or tamper with state (mass assignment).

Find all instances: Search for model binding/deserialization that maps request bodies onto domain entities, and check which authority-bearing fields are settable from input.

Fix correctly: Bind requests into explicit input DTOs containing only client-settable fields. Derive role/tenant/owner/pricing/status from trusted server-side state, never from the request. Apply allowlists for bindable fields.

Constraints: Prefer allowlists over denylists of fields. Validate at the boundary.

Acceptance: No authority-bearing field is settable from untrusted input. Add a test posting an elevated role/price field proving it is ignored.

checks.question: Are there queries, caches, jobs, files, queues, or events that are not scoped by tenant/account/workspace, allowing one tenant's data or actions to affect another (missing tenant isolation)? (IAM-005)

onYes.title: Fix missing tenant isolation (IAM-005): scope every operation by tenant
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Operations not scoped to a tenant can leak or cross-contaminate data between tenants.

Find all instances: Search data queries, cache keys, job/queue payloads, file paths, and event handlers for missing tenant/account/workspace scoping. Pay attention to shared caches and background jobs that derive tenant from data rather than the authenticated context.

Fix correctly: Derive the tenant from trusted context and scope every storage/service/cache/queue operation by it. Include tenant in cache keys and file paths. Enforce isolation at the storage boundary (e.g. filtered queries, row-level constraints).

Constraints: Do not derive tenant from client-supplied fields. Apply consistently across async/background paths.

Acceptance: Every operation is tenant-scoped at the storage/service boundary. Add a cross-tenant access test proving tenant A cannot reach tenant B's data.

checks.question: Are there endpoints where changing an ID, slug, filename, or key can expose another user's resource because access relies on the identifier being unguessable rather than on an authorization check (insecure direct object reference)? (IAM-006)

onYes.title: Fix IDOR (IAM-006): authorize resource access directly
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Relying on unguessable IDs instead of authorization lets attackers enumerate or guess identifiers to reach others' resources (IDOR).

Find all instances: Search for endpoints that return resources keyed by an ID/slug/filename/key from the request, including file download and report endpoints.

Fix correctly: Authorize access to the specific resource for the current principal on every request (scope queries by owner/tenant or check a policy). Treat unguessable IDs as defense-in-depth only.

Constraints: Apply to downloads and indirect references too. Centralize the check.

Acceptance: Resource access is authorized regardless of ID guessability. Add a test accessing another user's resource by ID proving denial.

checks.question: Does the codebase ship default passwords, bootstrap/sample admin accounts, or credentials documented as production-valid, instead of requiring secure first-run setup or managed identity? (IAM-007)

onYes.title: Fix default/admin credentials (IAM-007): require secure first-run setup
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Default or sample credentials are widely known and let attackers log in immediately.

Find all instances: Search source, config, seed/migration scripts, and docs for default passwords, bootstrap admin accounts, or 'change me' credentials usable in production.

Fix correctly: Remove built-in defaults. Require a secure first-run credential setup, or use managed/federated identity. If a seed account is needed for dev only, ensure it cannot exist in production builds/config.

Constraints: Do not hardcode any credential (config over hardcoding; secrets in managed storage). Rotate anything previously exposed.

Acceptance: No usable default/admin credential ships; first-run requires secure setup. Add a test/config check that production startup fails or requires setup rather than using a default.

checks.question: Do password, API-key, or token creation paths lack strong requirements for length/entropy and (where relevant) reuse and rotation, resulting in a weak credential policy? (IAM-008)

onYes.title: Fix weak credential policy (IAM-008): enforce strong credential requirements
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Weak credential requirements make brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks easy.

Find all instances: Search password/API-key/token creation and update flows for length, entropy, and reuse/rotation requirements.

Fix correctly: Enforce strong credentials (adequate length/entropy; check against known-breached lists where feasible). Prefer passkeys, MFA, or federated auth where appropriate. For API keys/tokens, generate with secure randomness and adequate length. Make policy values configurable.

Constraints: Config over hardcoding for policy thresholds. Do not weaken existing stronger requirements.

Acceptance: Credential creation enforces strong policy. Add tests rejecting weak/short/breached credentials and accepting compliant ones.

checks.question: Do login, token-issuance, password-reset, or verification-code flows lack rate limiting / lockout / abuse controls, leaving them open to credential stuffing and brute force? (IAM-009)

onYes.title: Fix missing credential-stuffing protection (IAM-009): rate-limit auth flows
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Without rate limits or lockouts, attackers can brute-force passwords, OTPs, and reset tokens at scale.

Find all instances: Search login, token, password-reset, and verification-code endpoints for rate limiting, lockout, and abuse detection.

Fix correctly: Add rate limits and progressive lockouts keyed by account and source, with MFA escalation and/or anomaly detection where appropriate. Use constant-time comparisons for codes/tokens. Make limits configurable.

Constraints: Avoid enabling account-lockout DoS; prefer adaptive throttling. Config over hardcoding for limits.

Acceptance: Auth/abuse-prone flows enforce rate limiting/lockout. Add a test proving repeated failed attempts are throttled/locked.

checks.question: Are there sensitive operations reachable without MFA even though MFA is required elsewhere, indicating inconsistent MFA enforcement? (IAM-010)

onYes.title: Fix inconsistent MFA enforcement (IAM-010): centralize MFA policy
onYes.prompt:
Problem: If some sensitive operations bypass MFA, attackers route around it.

Find all instances: Search privileged/sensitive operations and check MFA enforcement consistency against paths that do require it.

Fix correctly: Centralize MFA policy and apply it uniformly to all privileged paths (including alternate APIs, mobile, and admin tools). Re-prompt for MFA on step-up actions.

Constraints: Do not duplicate MFA checks inconsistently; centralize the decision.

Acceptance: MFA is enforced uniformly across all privileged paths. Add a test proving a sensitive operation cannot proceed without satisfied MFA.

checks.question: Do login or privilege-elevation flows keep the same session identifier after authentication (session fixation)? (IAM-011)

onYes.title: Fix session fixation (IAM-011): regenerate session ID after login
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Reusing a pre-auth session ID after login lets an attacker who planted that ID hijack the authenticated session (session fixation).

Find all instances: Search login, privilege-elevation, and account-linking flows for session ID regeneration after the security state changes.

Fix correctly: Regenerate the session identifier on login, privilege change, and account linking; invalidate the old session.

Constraints: Preserve necessary session data across regeneration. Use the framework's secure session APIs.

Acceptance: Session IDs are regenerated after authentication/privilege change. Add a test asserting the post-login session ID differs from the pre-login one.

checks.question: Are tokens, reset links, invitation codes, or session IDs generated using weak randomness, predictable inputs (timestamps/counters/hashes of public data), or sequential values rather than a cryptographically secure RNG with sufficient entropy? (IAM-012)

onYes.title: Fix predictable token generation (IAM-012): use a CSPRNG with sufficient entropy
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Predictable security tokens can be guessed, enabling account takeover or unauthorized access.

Find all instances: Search for generation of tokens, reset/magic links, invite codes, and session IDs. Flag use of non-cryptographic RNGs, timestamps, counters, or hashes of public data.

Fix correctly: Generate tokens with a cryptographically secure RNG and adequate length/entropy. Never roll your own randomness; use the platform CSPRNG. Store/compare tokens safely (constant-time, hashed at rest where appropriate).

Constraints: Never hand-roll crypto; use vetted primitives. Config over hardcoding for token length.

Acceptance: All security tokens use a CSPRNG with sufficient entropy. Add a test asserting tokens are non-sequential and of expected length/charset.

checks.question: Do logout, password reset, credential rotation, account deletion, or MFA changes leave previously issued sessions/tokens valid (session not invalidated)? (IAM-013)

onYes.title: Fix session not invalidated (IAM-013): revoke sessions on security changes
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Leaving old sessions valid after a security event means a compromised session survives password resets and logout.

Find all instances: Search logout, password-reset, credential-rotation, account-deletion, and MFA-change flows for session/token invalidation.

Fix correctly: Invalidate all affected sessions and refresh tokens after security-relevant changes (e.g. bump a per-user token version/epoch that is checked on each request).

Constraints: Ensure revocation propagates to stateless tokens (via version/epoch or a revocation list).

Acceptance: Security-relevant changes invalidate existing sessions/tokens. Add a test proving a token issued before a password reset is rejected afterward.

checks.question: Do access tokens, refresh tokens, reset links, magic links, or invitations have excessively long or missing expiry, without rotation/revocation/bounded reuse (excessive token lifetime)? (IAM-014)

onYes.title: Fix excessive token lifetime (IAM-014): short expiry with rotation and revocation
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Long-lived or non-expiring tokens widen the window for token theft and replay.

Find all instances: Search token/link/invitation issuance for expiry settings; flag missing or very long lifetimes and absent rotation/revocation.

Fix correctly: Use short access-token expiry with refresh-token rotation and revocation. Give reset/magic links and invitations short, single-use lifetimes. Make lifetimes configurable.

Constraints: Config over hardcoding for lifetimes. Do not break legitimate long-lived integration needs without an alternative (e.g. rotating keys).

Acceptance: Tokens/links have bounded, configurable expiry with rotation/revocation. Add tests proving an expired or already-used link/token is rejected.

checks.question: Does the codebase parse JWTs without verifying the signature, or in a way that accepts an attacker-controlled algorithm (e.g. 'none' or algorithm confusion)? (IAM-015)

onYes.title: Fix JWT signature/algorithm verification (IAM-015): pin alg and verify signature
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Accepting unverified or attacker-chosen-algorithm JWTs allows token forgery and full auth bypass.

Find all instances: Search JWT parsing/validation. Flag decode-without-verify, acceptance of 'none', and algorithm selected from the token header without a fixed expected algorithm/key.

Fix correctly: Verify the signature and enforce the expected algorithm, key, issuer, audience, and token type. Reject 'none'. Use a vetted JWT library; never hand-roll verification.

Constraints: Never hand-roll crypto. Pin the algorithm; do not trust the header alg.

Acceptance: JWTs are signature-verified with a fixed expected algorithm/key. Add tests rejecting an alg=none token and a token signed with the wrong key/algorithm.

checks.question: Does token validation check only the signature but not issuer, audience, expiry, subject, or scope (missing claim validation)? (IAM-016)

onYes.title: Fix missing claim validation (IAM-016): validate iss/aud/exp/scope
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Validating only the signature lets tokens minted for another service/audience be replayed against this one.

Find all instances: Search token validation for issuer, audience, expiry, subject, and scope/permission checks.

Fix correctly: Validate all security-relevant claims against this service's policy: expected issuer, audience, not-expired/not-before, subject, token type, and required scopes/permissions.

Constraints: Do not accept tokens for other audiences. Centralize validation policy.

Acceptance: All required claims are validated. Add tests rejecting tokens with wrong issuer/audience, expired tokens, and insufficient scope.

checks.question: Are there cookie-authenticated state-changing routes (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE or mutations) without CSRF protection (anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, origin checks, or non-cookie auth)? (IAM-017)

onYes.title: Fix CSRF on state-changing actions (IAM-017): add anti-CSRF protection
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Cookie-authenticated mutations without CSRF protection let a malicious site trigger actions as the logged-in user.

Find all instances: Search for state-changing endpoints that authenticate via cookies and check for CSRF defenses.

Fix correctly: Use anti-CSRF tokens and/or SameSite cookies and origin/referer validation; or use non-cookie auth (bearer tokens) for APIs. Apply consistently to all mutating cookie-auth endpoints.

Constraints: Keep safe methods (GET/HEAD) free of side effects (see API-006). Prefer framework CSRF middleware.

Acceptance: Cookie-authenticated mutations are CSRF-protected. Add a test asserting a state-changing request without a valid CSRF token/origin is rejected.

checks.question: Does CORS configuration allow credentials together with a wildcard, reflected, or overly broad set of origins (over-permissive credentialed CORS)? (IAM-018)

onYes.title: Fix over-permissive credentialed CORS (IAM-018): restrict origins explicitly
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Allowing credentials with wildcard/reflected origins lets any site make authenticated cross-origin requests and read responses.

Find all instances: Search CORS configuration for credentialed requests combined with wildcard origins, blind origin reflection, or overly broad allowed origins/methods/headers.

Fix correctly: Allow credentials only for an explicit allowlist of trusted origins; restrict allowed methods and headers. Never reflect arbitrary origins when credentials are allowed.

Constraints: Prefer allowlists over denylists. Make allowed origins configurable.

Acceptance: Credentialed CORS is limited to allowlisted origins. Add a test proving an untrusted origin is not granted credentialed access.

checks.question: Do signed webhooks, API requests, or callbacks lack nonce/timestamp/expiry/replay tracking, making them replay-prone? (IAM-019)

onYes.title: Fix replay-prone signed requests (IAM-019): add timestamp, nonce, and replay cache
onYes.prompt:
Problem: A valid signed request that lacks freshness controls can be captured and replayed.

Find all instances: Search signed webhook/API/callback verification for timestamp validation, nonce/idempotency checks, expiry, and replay tracking.

Fix correctly: Validate a signed timestamp within a small window, require a nonce/idempotency key tracked in a replay cache, and reject duplicates/expired requests. Verify the signature over the timestamp and body.

Constraints: Use constant-time signature comparison. Never hand-roll crypto.

Acceptance: Replayed signed requests are rejected. Add a test replaying a previously accepted signed request proving the second attempt fails.

checks.question: Is authorization logic duplicated and inconsistent across controllers, services, jobs, or APIs rather than centralized in one authorization layer, risking divergent/missing checks? (IAM-020)

onYes.title: Fix duplicated authorization logic (IAM-020): centralize policy decisions
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Scattered, copy-pasted permission checks drift apart, leaving gaps and inconsistencies attackers exploit.

Find all instances: Search for repeated ad hoc permission/role checks across controllers, services, jobs, and APIs.

Fix correctly: Centralize policy decisions in a single authorization layer/component and call it everywhere. Replace inline checks with calls to the shared policy.

Constraints: Do not change the intended access rules while refactoring; preserve behavior. Default deny.

Acceptance: Authorization decisions go through one shared layer. Add tests for representative allow/deny cases against the centralized policy and confirm callers use it.
